chapters.title: SQL: Creating and Altering Database and Tables

questions.question: What is a database? What is a DBMS? Explain the objectives/importance of DBMS.
questions.answer:
• A database is an organized collection of logically related data relevant to an enterprise — a repository of data files (university records, phone directory, banking data).
  • A DBMS is the software layer of programs used to store, retrieve and manipulate data conveniently and efficiently; it hides the underlying complexities of data management and provides an easy interface to users (examples: MySQL, Oracle, SQL Server, MS Access, DB2).
  • Objectives / importance:
    1. Reduce data redundancy — the same fact stored once, saving space and effort.
    2. Avoid inconsistency — changes propagate consistently instead of copies disagreeing.
    3. Share data among many users and applications without new stored files.
    4. Enforce integrity constraints (e.g., unique roll number).
    5. Enforce security — per-user, per-operation access control.
    6. Support transactions with commit/rollback.
    7. Backup and recovery to a previous consistent state.
    8. Concurrent access without inconsistency.

questions.question: Define a flat-file system. Discuss the merits and demerits of a DBMS compared with traditional file-based storage.
questions.answer:
• Flat file system: each application stores its own separate files; data is duplicated across files and programs navigate records directly.
  • Merits of DBMS: controls redundancy; consistency; data sharing; integrity, security and standards enforced centrally; backup/recovery; concurrent access; independence of data from programs.
  • Demerits: high initial cost (software, hardware, training); extra complexity of design and administration; overhead for simple applications; risk of a single point of failure; conversion cost from legacy files.

questions.question: List and explain different applications of DBMS.
questions.answer:
• Banking: accounts, loans, transactions, fraud monitoring.
  • Airlines/railways: reservations, schedules, passenger records.
  • Universities: students, courses, results, registration.
  • Telecommunications: call records, billing, network data.
  • E-commerce: catalogs, orders, customers, inventory.
  • Manufacturing/HR: production and payroll records; also library systems, hospitals and social networks.

questions.question: Explain the three-level (three-schema) architecture of a database with a diagram.
questions.answer:
The DBMS separates the database description into three levels:

  • Internal level (physical schema): how data is physically stored — file organizations, blocks, access paths and indexes.
  • Conceptual level (logical schema): the community view: entities, attributes, relationships, constraints — what data is stored and its structure.
  • External level (view level): individual user/application views hiding the rest of the conceptual schema.
  • Mappings between levels maintain independence: changes at one level need not affect the others.
 external views      view 1        view 2        view 3
                        \            |            /
 conceptual level      conceptual schema
 internal level        physical schema (files, indexes)

questions.question: How is logical data independence different from physical data independence? *(3–5 marks)*
questions.answer:
• Logical data independence: ability to change the conceptual schema (add/remove tables, columns) without changing external views or application programs.
  • Physical data independence: ability to change the internal schema (storage structures, file organization, indexes) without changing the conceptual schema.
  • Logical independence is harder to achieve because views derive from the conceptual schema.

questions.question: What is a data model? Describe its types — hierarchical, network, relational, object-oriented.
questions.answer:
A data model is a collection of concepts for describing data, its relationships, semantics and constraints.

  • Hierarchical model: records form a tree of parent–child links (one-to-many, one parent per child). Simple and fast for tree data (IBM IMS), but rigid for many-to-many data.
  • Network model: records and relationships form a graph; owner–member "sets" support many-to-many; more flexible, more complex to design and navigate (CODASYL/DBTG).
  • Relational model: data is stored as relations (tables) of rows and columns; relationships by shared values (keys); queried with relational algebra and SQL. Simple, flexible, dominant today.
  • Object-oriented model: data and behaviour encapsulated in objects with identity, attributes and methods; supports complex data (frames, students in OODB/ORDB).

questions.question: What is the ER model? Explain entity, attribute, strong vs weak entity set.
questions.answer:
• The Entity-Relationship model is a high-level conceptual data model that describes data as entities, their attributes and relationships, drawn as an ER diagram.
  • Entity: a real-world object or concept (Student, Course); attribute: a property of an entity (roll no, name); relationship: an association between entities.
  • Strong entity set: has its own key attribute, exists independently (e.g., Bank with code).
  • Weak entity set: has no key of its own; it is identified by the owner entity and a partial key; drawn with a double rectangle and connected by a double diamond, with total participation in the identifying relationship (e.g., Loan of a Customer).

questions.question: Differentiate generalization and aggregation with examples.
questions.answer:
• Generalization: a bottom-up abstraction that combines common properties of several lower-level entity sets into a higher-level superclass — e.g., Car and Truck generalize to Vehicle (IS-A relationship).
  • Aggregation: an abstraction that treats a relationship between entities as a higher-level entity so it can participate in another relationship — e.g., a Project uses a Machine; the combination of Employee-works-on- Project is aggregated when another relationship (e.g., monitors) needs it.

questions.question: Roles and responsibilities of a DBA.
questions.answer:
• Define and maintain the conceptual/internal schemas; decide storage structures and access methods.
  • Grant/revoke user authorizations and enforce security policy.
  • Monitor performance and tune the database; plan capacity.
  • Maintain backups and plan recovery; manage upgrades and standards.
  • Liaise with users on data requirements and documentation.

questions.question: Explain unary, binary and ternary relationships (degree of a relationship).
questions.answer:
The degree of a relationship is the number of entity sets that participate in it.

  • Unary (recursive) relationship: one entity set is related to itself — e.g., an Employee manages another Employee, or a Course has another Course as prerequisite. Roles (manager/subordinate) distinguish the participants.
  • Binary relationship: two entity sets participate — the most common kind (Student enrolls in Course, Customer places Order).
  • Ternary relationship: three entity sets participate simultaneously — e.g., Supplier supplies Part to Project (a shipment), or Doctor prescribes Drug to Patient; a diamond connects three entity sets, and the relationship may carry its own attributes (quantity, date).

Most ER diagrams are built from binary relationships; unary and ternary relationships are used when the same set or three sets interact directly.

questions.question: Define/differentiate keys: super key, candidate key, primary key, foreign key, composite key, partial key.
questions.answer:
• Super key: any attribute set that uniquely identifies a tuple (e.g., {Roll, Name}).
  • Candidate key: a minimal super key — no proper subset identifies tuples (e.g., Roll).
  • Primary key: the candidate key chosen by the designer to identify tuples; it is unique and NOT NULL.
  • Foreign key: attribute(s) in one relation that reference the primary key of another relation; enforces referential integrity.
  • Composite key: a key made of two or more attributes (e.g., {BookId, CardNo} of BookIssue).
  • Partial key: an attribute that distinguishes weak-entity instances of the same owner (drawn dotted in the ER diagram).

questions.question: Define union compatibility. Show Director ∩ Actor and Actor ∪ Director for the given relations.
questions.answer:
Two tables are union compatible if they have the same number of attributes and corresponding attributes have the same data type. Then set operations are defined:

  • Director ∩ Actor returns the tuples present in both relations.
  • Actor ∪ Director returns all tuples, duplicates removed.
  • Both operations require union compatibility; for the printed example, ∩ = {Deepak Giri, Bhuwan KC} and ∪ = {Deepak Giri, Bhuwan KC, Rajesh Hamal, Dipendra Khanal} (row order as printed in the solved book).

questions.question: Explain selection and projection. Using Student and Department joined on Did, write relational algebra returning Fname for Bachelor students living in Birgunj whose department head is Ramesh Sharma.
questions.answer:
• Selection (σ): keeps rows satisfying a condition — σLevel='Bachelor'(Student).
  • Projection (π): keeps the named columns, removing duplicates — πFname, Lname(Student).
  • Join: combines matching rows of two relations; union/intersection/ difference are set operations on union-compatible relations.
  • 2022 RA query (students in 'Bachelor' living in 'Birgunj' under department head 'Ramesh Sharma'):
πFname(σLevel='Bachelor' ∧ Address='Birgunj' ∧ HOD='Ramesh Sharma' (Student JOIN ON Student.Did = Department.Did Department))

Equivalently: select the qualifying Department rows first, join with Student on Did, then project Fname.

questions.question: Given Sailors/Boats/Reserves, write RA and SQL for the five listed queries.
questions.answer:
• a) Name, rating, age of all sailors: SELECT sname, rating, age FROM Sailors; / πsname,rating,age(Sailors).
  • b) Boats having color blue: SELECT bname, color FROM Boats WHERE color = 'blue'; / πbname,colour(σcolour='blue'(Boats)).
  • c) Boats reserved on a given date: join Reserves with Boats on bid and filter reservedate.
  • d) Boats and sailors who reserved green boats: SELECT s.sname, b.bname FROM Sailors s, Reserves r, Boats b WHERE s.sid = r.sid AND r.bid = b.bid AND b.colour = 'green';.
  • e) Outer joins: Sailors LEFT OUTER JOIN Reserves ON Sailors.sid = Reserves.sid; and the RIGHT OUTER JOIN counterpart — unmatched rows keep NULLs on the other side.

questions.question: Differentiate DDL and DML. Given Borrower(Customer name, Loan number) and Loan(Loan number, Branch name, Amount), write relational algebra finding customers who borrowed from branch B1.
questions.answer:
• DDL: define/modify the structure — CREATE, ALTER, DROP, TRUNCATE.
  • DML: manipulate the data — SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE.
  • RA for "customers who took a loan from branch B1" (Borrower(Customer name, Loan number), Loan(Loan number, Branch name, Amount)):
πCustomer name(σBranch name='B1'(Borrower JOIN Loan))

questions.question: Why is normalization needed? What are the anomalies?
questions.answer:
• Normalization is the process of eliminating the flaws of a poorly designed database; it removes redundant data (storage efficiency, integrity, scalability) and ensures dependencies make sense (only related data stored together).
  • It fixes insert, update and delete anomalies and keeps the structure flexible, at the cost of more relations/joins.
  • Insert anomaly: cannot insert some facts because key values are missing.
  • Update anomaly: a repeated fact must be updated in many rows and copies can disagree.
  • Deletion anomaly: deleting a row destroys unrelated vital facts stored with it.

questions.question: Explain functional dependencies and normal forms 1NF, 2NF, 3NF, BCNF (and 4NF) with examples. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer:
• Functional dependency X → Y: each value of X determines exactly one value of Y (e.g., Roll → Name). Types: trivial, non-trivial; partial (part of a composite key determines an attribute) and transitive (X → Y and Y → Z imply X → Z) dependencies cause 2NF/3NF violations.
  • 1NF: every attribute value is atomic; no repeating groups. Convert Student(Sid, Sname, Subjects(Sub1, Sub2)) into one row per subject or a separate subject relation.
  • 2NF: in 1NF and no partial dependency on the key. For Employee-Department(Emp-Id, Emp-Name, Emp-Salary, Dept-No, Dept-Name) with key (Emp-Id, Dept-No), Emp-Name/Salary depend only on Emp-Id and Dept-Name only on Dept-No → split into Employee and Department.
  • 3NF: in 2NF and no transitive dependency of non-prime attributes. Student(Sid, Sex, Hostel-Name) with Sid → Sex, Sex → Hostel-Name → split into Student(Sid, Sex?)/Hostel(Sex, Hostel-Name) (as printed) or keep a hostel id.
  • BCNF: for every non-trivial FD X → Y, X is a super key. Removes anomalies from overlapping candidate keys that 3NF misses.
  • 4NF: in BCNF and no non-trivial multivalued dependency; relevant when independent multivalued facts sit in one relation.

questions.question: Convert a given unnormalized table into BCNF step by step. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer: flattening repeating groups; (2) remove partial dependencies → decompose to 2NF; (3) remove transitive dependencies → 3NF; (4) check every determinant is a super key → decompose to BCNF; verify all keys preserved. Apply to the given table with its stated FDs; each decomposition splits the offending FD's determinant and dependents into a new relation.

questions.question: SQL constraints: create/alter tables with PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, CHECK, DEFAULT; DROP and ALTER.
questions.answer:
CREATE TABLE Student (
  Roll   INT PRIMARY KEY,
  Name   VARCHAR(40) NOT NULL,
  Age    INT CHECK (Age >= 17),
  Status VARCHAR(10) DEFAULT 'active',
  DeptId INT REFERENCES Department(DeptId)
);

ALTER TABLE Student ADD Email VARCHAR(60);
ALTER TABLE Student MODIFY Age INT CHECK (Age BETWEEN 17 AND 40);
DROP TABLE Old_Results;
  • PRIMARY KEY: unique + NOT NULL identifier; FOREIGN KEY/REFERENCES: referential integrity; CHECK: value predicate; DEFAULT: value when omitted; NOT NULL/UNIQUE.
  • ALTER modifies structure (add/modify/drop columns, constraints); DROP removes a table/column or its definition. DDL changes are auto-committed.

questions.question: Explain INSERT, SELECT, UPDATE, DELETE with examples.
questions.answer:
INSERT INTO Student (Roll, Name, Age) VALUES (1, 'Sita', 19);
SELECT Name, Age FROM Student WHERE Age > 18 ORDER BY Name ASC;
UPDATE Student SET Age = 20 WHERE Roll = 1;
DELETE FROM Student WHERE Roll = 1;
  • SELECT returns a result table; WHERE filters rows, ORDER BY sorts, GROUP BY groups for aggregate functions, HAVING filters groups.

questions.question: How are ORDER BY and GROUP BY / HAVING different?
questions.answer:
• ORDER BY sorts the final result set by one or more columns (ASC/DESC, default ASC), applied after the result is produced.
  • GROUP BY groups rows that share values of the grouping columns so aggregate functions (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN) compute per group; HAVING then filters whole groups (WHERE filters individual rows before grouping).
  • Example: SELECT Dept, COUNT(*) FROM Student GROUP BY Dept HAVING COUNT(*) > 5 ORDER BY Dept;

questions.question: Different types of JOINS in SQL with examples. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer:
• INNER JOIN: matching rows only — A JOIN B on the join condition.
  • LEFT/RIGHT OUTER JOIN: keep unmatched rows of the left/right table with NULLs on the other side.
  • FULL OUTER JOIN: keep unmatched rows from both sides.
  • NATURAL JOIN: joins on all common column names.
  • CROSS JOIN: Cartesian product; SELF JOIN: a table joined to itself.
  • Example: SELECT s.sname, b.bname FROM Sailors s INNER JOIN Reserves r ON s.sid=r.sid INNER JOIN Boats b ON r.bid=b.bid WHERE b.colour='blue';

questions.question: Nested query; SQL/RA query sets (book-borrower, supplier, restaurant).
questions.answer:
• Nested query: a subquery inside another query (WHERE, FROM or SELECT); e.g. borrowers of books priced above average: SELECT Name FROM Borrower WHERE Card_No IN (SELECT CardNo FROM BookIssue WHERE BookId IN (SELECT Bookid FROM Book WHERE Price > (SELECT AVG(Price) FROM Book)));
  • Typical 10-mark sets follow the printed answers: suppliers/parts (create table, quantities, parts by "RD Traders", count by "S02", suppliers in "KTM"); books/borrowers (books taken by Ramesh Sharma; issued titles with date windows; author Laxmi Prashad Devkota; count on 25 April 2023; above average price); restaurant/cook/food: SELECT Rname, Rlocation FROM Restaurant; SELECT Workinghrs FROM Worksat WHERE Cname='Sita'; SELECT Fname FROM Food WHERE Cname='Ramesh'; SELECT Rname FROM Restaurant NATURAL JOIN Food WHERE Category='breakfast'; SELECT Cname FROM Worksat WHERE Rname='KFC';

questions.question: What is a stored procedure? Advantages; parameters; create/execute with an example. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer:
• A stored procedure is a named PL/SQL block, stored in the database, that accepts parameters, performs one or more operations and may return a value. Advantages: multiple operations in one call; central business rules; easier maintenance/testing; reduced network traffic; reusable and secure (privileges on the procedure, not tables).
  • Parameter modes: IN (read-only input), OUT (output only), IN OUT (both).
  • Example:
  CREATE OR REPLACE PROCEDURE Stu_info AS
    sname VARCHAR(20) := 'Bhupi'; age NUMBER := 33;
  BEGIN
    DBMS_OUTPUT.PUT_LINE('My name = ' || sname || ' Age= ' || age);
  END;
  -- execute
  SET SERVEROUTPUT ON;
  EXECUTE Stu_info;

questions.question: Differentiate stored procedure and trigger; types of triggers; before/after INSERT trigger. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer:
• Stored procedure: called explicitly by the user/application; may take parameters; does not fire on its own.
  • Trigger: fires automatically when its event (INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE) and timing occur; no direct invocation, cannot return values; used for audit trails, derived data and business rules.
  • Types: row vs statement; BEFORE vs AFTER; INSTEAD OF (views).
  • Example:
  CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER Product_audit
  AFTER INSERT ON Products FOR EACH ROW
  BEGIN
    INSERT INTO Product_log (pid, log_date)
    VALUES (:NEW.pid, SYSDATE);
  END;

questions.question: Why is indexing essential? Differentiate dense and sparse index; create with SQL.
questions.answer:
• An index is an auxiliary access structure (search key + pointer) that speeds up retrieval, range searches and joins; without it the DBMS scans all records. Cost: extra space and maintenance on updates.
  • Dense index: one entry per search-key value/record — faster lookups, more space.
  • Sparse index: one entry per block (file must be ordered by the search key) — smaller, but a block scan follows the lookup.
  • SQL: CREATE INDEX idx_student_name ON Student(Name); CREATE UNIQUE INDEX idx_roll ON Student(Roll);

questions.question: How is the cost of a query measured? Construct a query expression tree.
questions.answer:
• Query cost is measured by the resources consumed: number of disk block accesses/transfers (dominant), CPU time, and communication cost in distributed systems; optimisation estimates these from statistics (cardinality, block counts, selectivity).
  • Expression tree: leaves are relations; internal nodes are relational algebra operators (σ, π, JOIN, ×, ∪...); evaluation order is chosen to minimise intermediate sizes. Example (2018):
  ΠLFName, LName, Address
      |
      σDName='Research'
          |
          JOIN Dnumber=Dno
         /            \
   Department        ×
                    /   \
              Employee  Works_on

Moving selections below joins (push-down) reduces cost.

questions.question: Materialized vs pipelined evaluation; query optimization process.
questions.answer:
• Materialized evaluation: compute an operation fully, store the result in a temporary relation, feed the next operator — simple, but temp I/O adds cost.
  • Pipelined evaluation: pass tuples directly from one operator to the next — no (or fewer) temp relations, lower cost, first results sooner, needs buffers.
  • Optimization process: parse/validate → translate to relational algebra → generate logically equivalent expression trees → estimate costs with statistics → choose the cheapest plan → execute. Heuristics (push selections/projections down, choose join order) plus cost-based choice.

questions.question: Database security; discretionary vs mandatory access control; security measures.
questions.answer:
• Discretionary access control (DAC): owners grant/revoke privileges on objects (GRANT/REVOKE); flexible but vulnerable to Trojan horses.
  • Mandatory access control (MAC): system-wide classification (Top Secret → Public) with clearance rules; users cannot override.
  • Measures: authentication (passwords, biometrics), authorization and views, encryption of data/in-transit, auditing and logging, backups, integrity constraints, and physical security. Security applies to each access type (retrieve, modify, delete).

questions.question: Describe the steps of query processing.
questions.answer:
1. Parsing and translation: check syntax/semantics, convert to relational algebra.
  2. Optimization: choose an efficient execution plan among equivalents using cost estimates.
  3. Evaluation: run the plan (scanning, sorting, joining, indexing) and return results. (Security/catalog checks run with parsing.)

questions.question: Explain transaction states and ACID properties.
questions.answer:
• A transaction is a set of logically related operations (e.g., transfer Rs 500 between accounts) executed as one unit.
  • States: Active → Partially committed → Committed → Terminated; failures move to Failed → Aborted (rolled back, possibly restarted).
  • ACID: Atomicity (all or nothing), Consistency (valid state to valid state), Isolation (concurrent transactions do not interfere), Durability (committed changes survive failure).

questions.question: Read/write operations in a transaction.
questions.answer: • READ(X) fetches X from the database into the transaction's workspace; WRITE(X) writes the workspace value back after the last write. A schedule is the ordered sequence of such operations; serial schedules run transactions one after another.

questions.question: Concurrency control: why needed; two-phase locking; timestamp ordering; serializability. *(5–10 marks)*
questions.answer:
• Concurrency control prevents interference anomalies (lost update, dirty read, unrepeatable read) and keeps schedules serializable (equivalent to some serial order).
  • Two-phase locking (2PL): a growing phase where locks are only acquired and a shrinking phase where locks are only released; guarantees conflict-serializability. Strict 2PL holds exclusive locks until commit.
  • Timestamp ordering: each transaction gets a timestamp; conflicting operations execute in timestamp order (older first). Read(X) rejected if W_TS(X) > TS(Ti); Write(X) rejected and Ti rolled back if TS(Ti) < R_TS(X) or TS(Ti) < W_TS(X); otherwise execute and update the item's timestamps (worked example: TS(T1)=100, TS(T2)=110 → T1 aborted to avoid a lost update).
  • Deadlock: cycle of transactions waiting for each other's locks; detected via wait-for-graph cycles; prevented by timestamps (wait-die/wound-wait) or avoided via timeouts; recovered by aborting a victim.

questions.question: Lost update and dirty read problems with examples.
questions.answer:
• Lost update: T1 and T2 both read X, both update it and write; the second write overwrites the first, so T1's update is lost.
  • Dirty read: T1 updates X, T2 reads the new X before T1 commits/rolls back; when T1 aborts, T2's read was based on a value that never became stable — T2 is "dirty".

questions.question: Design an ER diagram (university/hospital/car-insurance/shipment); participation and cardinality; convert to tables.
questions.answer:
Method: list entities and attributes (underline primary keys), choose relationships with cardinality (1:1, 1:N, M:N), mark total participation with double lines (e.g., every policy has payments) and partial with single lines, add identifying relationships for weak entities, then convert:

  • strong entities → tables with their key;
  • M:N relationships → a table with the keys of both sides;
  • 1:N relationships → the key of the "1" side added to the "N" side's table;
  • multivalued attributes → separate tables;
  • weak entities → table with owner key + partial key.

(For the printed worked example see model-01 p. 6–7: Bank/Branch/Account/ Loan/Customer → tables.)
